points.quote: shared locks on what it reads and exclusive locks on what it writes
points.problem: Shared and exclusive locks are used as known terms. Nothing earlier in the book says what separates them (many readers together, one writer alone), so the reader cannot see why a reader and a writer would conflict, which is the point the MVCC contrast depends on.
points.hint: Add a clause: a shared lock lets other readers in but keeps writers out; an exclusive lock keeps everyone else out.

points.quote: descend from one of two 1970s prototypes, System R at IBM San Jose or Ingres
points.problem: Oracle is counted as a descendant of System R here, and the Fig 13.1 caption says it came 'through IBM's published SQL'. Section p5 says Ellison built Oracle from Codd's paper, and p6 says MySQL and others were 'written fresh to speak the SQL that System R introduced'. The reader cannot tell how Oracle's relation to System R differs from MySQL's, or whether it read Codd or IBM's papers.
points.hint: Either name Oracle with the 'written fresh to speak SQL' group, or say in one clause what Oracle took from System R's published SQL.

points.quote: InnoDB follows the same redo-and-undo shape
points.problem: In the strip, InnoDB appears with no hint that it is MySQL's storage engine, and its ARIES, redo-only and MVCC contrast leans on terms the reader has not met yet ('explained below'). A newcomer opening the strip hits unglossed names.
points.hint: Write 'MySQL's InnoDB engine' at first mention.
